figures.cap: right-angled triangle ABT with right angle at B, angle 26 degrees at A, height h

parts.latex:
A tower $BT$ has height $h$ metres.

From point $A$, the angle of elevation to the top of the tower is $26^\circ$ as shown.

\exfigure{268_q3_1}

Which of the following is the correct expression for the length of $AB$?

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $ABT$, $BT$ is opposite the $26^\circ$ angle and $AB$ is adjacent:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 26^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{AB} \\ AB &= \dfrac{h}{\tan 26^\circ} \\ &= h\cot 26^\circ \end{aligned}$$

613.stem:
A helicopter leaves Underwood and flies 70 km on a bearing of $055^\circ$ to Vacy.

It then flies 82 km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to Woodville.

The diagram below illustrates the journey.

\exfigure{1369_q19_1}

figures.cap: solution sketch: bearings diagram with 55 and 30 degree angles and theta at W

parts.latex:
The helicopter then plans to fly directly to Underwood.

Calculate, to the nearest km, the distance that it will fly.

Determine the bearing (from Woodville) on which it should fly to return to Underwood.

Give your answer to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1369_q19_s1}

$\angle UVW=55^\circ+30^\circ=85^\circ$ (co-interior angles with the north lines).

By the cosine rule in $\triangle UVW$:
$$\begin{aligned}UW^2&=70^2+82^2-2\times 70\times 82\cos 85^\circ\\ &=10623.45\ldots\\ UW&=103.07\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ It will fly $103$ km (nearest km).
criteria: Correct use of cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $\angle UWV=\theta$. By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta&=\dfrac{103^2+82^2-70^2}{2\times 103\times 82}\\ &=0.736\ldots\\ \theta&=42.605\ldots^\circ\\ &\approx 43^\circ\ \text{(nearest degree)}\end{aligned}$$
The bearing of $V$ from $W$ is $360^\circ-30^\circ$, and $U$ is a further $43^\circ$ anticlockwise, so the bearing from $W$ to $U$ is
$$360^\circ-30^\circ-43^\circ=287^\circ\text{T}$$

647.stem: Joshua and Fahim leave base camp ($C$) together and walk on a bearing of $100^\circ T$ for 10 km to a waterfall ($W$). Joshua stays at the waterfall and Fahim continues his journey by walking 6 km on a bearing of $258^\circ T$ to a lookout ($L$).

figures.cap: unlabelled triangle with north lines, NOT TO SCALE
solution sketch: triangle CWL with bearings 100 and 258 degrees, CW=10 km, WL=6 km

parts.latex:
Complete the diagram by showing all information.

\exfigure{1356_q22_1}
Find the distance between the lookout and base camp. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
Hence, or otherwise find the bearing that Fahim must walk on, to return to the base camp.

Cosine rule.evidence: Finds ∠WLC using the cosine rule or the sine rule
Cosine rule.reason: Criterion accepts cosine rule or sine rule: free choice of method.

Sine rule.evidence: Finds ∠WLC using the cosine rule or the sine rule
Sine rule.reason: Criterion accepts cosine rule or sine rule: free choice of method.

solutions.latex:
The bearing of $L$ from $W$ is $258^\circ$, so measured anticlockwise from north:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle NWL+258^\circ&=360^\circ\\\angle NWL&=102^\circ\end{aligned}$$
The bearing of $C$ from $W$ is $280^\circ$, so $\angle NWC=80^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle CWL&=102^\circ-80^\circ\\&=22^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle CWL$, $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$:
$$\begin{aligned}CL^2&=10^2+6^2-2\times 10\times 6\cos 22^\circ\\&=24.73793745\\CL&=4.973724706\\&\approx 4.97\text{ km}\ (2\text{ decimal places})\end{aligned}$$

Using the cosine rule in $\triangle CWL$ to find $\angle WLC$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\angle WLC&=\dfrac{CL^2+WL^2-CW^2}{2\times CL\times WL}\\&=\dfrac{4.97\ldots^2+6^2-10^2}{2\times 4.97\ldots\times 6}\\&=-0.6578246162\\\angle WLC&=131.1341759^\circ\\&\approx 131^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$\angle NWL=102^\circ$ (part (b)), and the north lines at $W$ and $L$ are parallel:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle WLN&=180^\circ-102^\circ\\&=78^\circ\quad(\text{co-interior angles})\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\angle NLC&=131^\circ-78^\circ\\&=53^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$C$ is $53^\circ$ anticlockwise from north at $L$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Bearing}&=360^\circ-53^\circ\\&=307^\circ T\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle WLC$ using the cosine rule or the sine rule, or equivalent merit
Finds an expression for $\cos\angle WLC$ or $\sin\angle WLC$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the angle $131^\circ-78^\circ=53^\circ$ was labelled $\angle NWL$; it is $\angle NLC$ (at $L$).

708.stem:
Sally is training for the swim leg of a triathlon and decides to go for a training swim in the harbour. She starts at a jetty $J$ and swims on a bearing of $105^\circ$ for 5 km out to a buoy $L$. She then changes direction and swims on a bearing of $045^\circ$ for a further 16 km to buoy $M$.

\exfigure{1363_q23_1}

figures.cap: bearings diagram: J to L 5 km on 105 degrees, L to M 16 km on 045 degrees; NOT TO SCALE

parts.latex: Find the distance $JM$ that Sally will swim back to the jetty.
Find the bearing of jetty $J$ from the buoy $L$.

solutions.latex:
The north lines at $J$ and $L$ are parallel, so the angle between $LJ$ and north at $L$ is $180^\circ-105^\circ=75^\circ$ (co-interior angles). $LM$ is $45^\circ$ on the other side of north:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle JLM&=75^\circ+45^\circ\\ &=120^\circ \end{aligned}$$

Cosine rule in $\triangle JLM$:
$$\begin{aligned} JM^2&=5^2+16^2-2\times5\times16\times\cos 120^\circ\\ &=361\\ JM&=19\text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From (a), $LJ$ is $75^\circ$ anticlockwise from north at $L$; bearings are measured clockwise from north:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing}&=360^\circ-75^\circ\\ &=285^\circ \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: Brooklyn 11 km north of Camp, Milan 12 km east of Camp; NOT TO SCALE

parts.latex:
At 9 am, Brooklyn is 11 km due north of camp, while Milan is 12 km due east of camp. Their positions are shown on the diagram below.

\exfigure{1357_q14_1}

They both start walking directly towards camp at a speed of 4 kilometres per hour.

Find the distance between Brooklyn and Milan at 11 am.

solutions.latex:
In 2 hours each walks $2 \times 4 = 8$ km towards camp.

At 11 am Brooklyn is $11 - 8 = 3$ km from camp and Milan is $12 - 8 = 4$ km from camp.

By Pythagoras' theorem (north and east are at right angles):
$$\begin{aligned} d &= \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} \\ &= 5 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of Pythagoras' theorem with the new distances, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: two poles of heights 8 m and 25 m at B and C, viewed from A

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangles at the bases of the poles, using the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan 61^\circ&=\dfrac{25}{AC} & \tan 37^\circ&=\dfrac{8}{AB}\\ AC&=\dfrac{25}{\tan 61^\circ} & AB&=\dfrac{8}{\tan 37^\circ}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}BC&=AC-AB\\&=\dfrac{25}{\tan 61^\circ}-\dfrac{8}{\tan 37^\circ}\\&=25\cot 61^\circ-8\cot 37^\circ\end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: Wheel with centre O touching the track at M, arrow showing direction of rolling
solution sketch: Wheel after rolling, M' above the track with right triangle at O, height h

parts.latex: Through what angle does $M$ rotate about $O$ (in radians) after the wheel rolls 1 metre ?
After the wheel rolls 1 metre, what is the vertical height of $M$ above the track? (answer to the nearest cm)

Arc length.evidence: The angle in the right-angled triangle is 5/2−π/2
Arc length.reason: Rolling 1 m gives θ=100/40=5/2 rad via l=rθ.

solutions.latex:
Using the arc length formula $l=r\theta$, with $l=100$ cm and $r=40$ cm:
$$\begin{aligned} 100 &= 40\theta \\ \theta &= \dfrac{5}{2} \text{ radians} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{377_q18_s1}

$M'$ is where $M$ rolls to, and $h$ is the height of $M'$ above the track.

The angle in the right-angled triangle is $\dfrac{5}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}$ radians.

In this triangle, $\sin\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}=\dfrac{x}{40}$, so
$$x=40\sin\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} h &= 40+x \\ &= 40+40\sin\left(\dfrac{5-\pi}{2}\right) \\ &\approx 72.0457 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=72 \text{ cm (nearest cm)}$$
criteria: Finds the correct expression for $x$, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct angle in the triangle, or equivalent merit
